# Bar

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

How large is each category? `bar` draws a rectangle from the baseline (zero) to
the value for each row. Bars are vertical when the categories are on `x` and
horizontal when they are on `y`; see [Horizontal bars](#horizontal-bars).

The bar chart exists because William Playfair had too little data. His
*Commercial and Political Atlas* of 1786 drew England's imports and exports as
two curves across thirty years [@playfair1786]. For Scotland he had a single
year, and no curve can show one year. So he drew a bar for each of Scotland's
trading partners instead, and wrote that the result was a weaker picture than a curve,
because it showed no change over time. The form he apologized for became the
one everyone knows.

Two names for it are still in use, and they name opposite orientations. Much of
the business world, Excel included, calls this a **column chart** when the bars
are vertical, and uses **bar chart** only when they are horizontal. gog has one
`bar`, and its direction comes from whichever axis carries the category. A
third name, **histogram**, belongs to a different plot drawn with the same
mark. Karl Pearson introduced the word in the 1890s [@pearson1895] for the
picture of a *distribution*. Its bars cover intervals cut from a continuous
axis, and neighboring bars touch. In gog that plot is `bar * bin`, shown in
[Histogram](#histogram) below.

## Basic usage {#basic-usage}

Which country won the most gold medals? Most examples in this chapter start from
the smallest sentence that draws a bar: a source, the mark, and its two
positions. The `medals` table holds one row for each of five countries, and
each row gives the number of Olympic gold, silver and bronze medals that
country won.
[The book's data](../book-data.qmd) describes it and every other table in the
book.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(medals)
```

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold)
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold."*

The x axis places a tick at each bar position automatically. The y axis reaches
zero unless you state your own `limits`, so a bar's length is its value.

## Color {#color}

Every bar is the same color until you map a column to `color`. With a color for
each bar, a reader can find one country quickly and match it to the same
country in another plot, as long as that plot also colors by country. Bind
`color` to the column that is already on `x`, and `color` fills each bar with a
distinct color:

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  color(country)
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, color by country."*

The legend repeats the names on the x axis, because the same column is on
both. `color(country, legend = FALSE)` keeps the colors and [leaves the legend
out](../channels.qmd#leaving-a-legend-out).

## Ordering bars {#ordering-bars}

In what order should the bars appear? A reader looking for the largest value
wants it first. A reader looking for one name wants the names in alphabetical
order. `order()` controls the sequence of categories along whichever axis
carries them: `x` on a vertical plot, `y` on a horizontal one. You can sort on
the categorical column itself, on the measured column, or on a third column of
numbers. After `bar * count`, you can also sort on the count. Naming the
categorical column asks for that column's own order. Here that is alphabetical,
because `order()` sorts plain text such as `country` from A to Z. A column with a
[declared order](../data.qmd#declaring-the-order-of-categories) uses that order
instead.

**Default, data order** (rows as they appear in the table) is the order of the
plot in [Basic usage](#basic-usage).

**By value, descending**, tallest bar first, the usual order for a ranking:

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) +
  title("Gold medals: largest first")
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, largest
first."*

These bars are in the same order as the plot in [Basic usage](#basic-usage).
The medals table already lists the country with the most gold first, so ordering by gold
changes nothing here. Writing the order anyway is still safer, because the plot
then stays sorted even if next year's table lists the countries in a different
order. The
plots below each put the bars in a different order.

**By value, ascending**, smallest first, useful when scanning for the lowest
values:

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold) +
  title("Gold medals: smallest first")
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, smallest
first."*

**By category name, A → Z**, natural for names and labels:

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(country) +
  title("Gold medals: A to Z")
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by country, A to
Z."*

**By category name, Z → A**, the reverse:

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(country, desc = TRUE) +
  title("Gold medals: Z to A")
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by country, Z to
A."*

**By a third column**, order countries by their silver medal count, while
plotting gold:

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(silver, desc = TRUE) +
  title("Gold medals: ordered by silver")
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by silver, largest
first."*

**By the count**, when each bar is a count of rows. The `gapminder_2007` table
holds one row for each of 142 countries in 2007. Each row gives the country's
continent, its life expectancy (`life`), its population and its GDP per person
(`gdp`). The [`count` transform](../transforms.qmd#count-frequency-aggregation),
written `bar * count`, draws how many countries each continent has:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  order(count, desc = TRUE) +
  title("Countries per continent: largest first")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, ordered by count,
largest first."*

Africa, with 52 countries, comes first, and Oceania, with 2, comes last. The
table has no `count` column. `bar * count` writes one, and `order()` names it
like any other column of numbers. After `bar * proportion`, write
`order(proportion)` in the same way. The Transforms chapter
[draws that plot](../transforms.qmd#proportion-relative-frequency).

| Expression | Order |
|-----------|-------|
| *(none)* | Data order (rows as they appear) |
| `order(gold)` | Ascending by gold (smallest first) |
| `order(gold, desc = TRUE)` | Descending by gold (largest first) |
| `order(country)` | A → Z by country name |
| `order(country, desc = TRUE)` | Z → A by country name |
| `order(silver, desc = TRUE)` | By another column of numbers |
| `order(count, desc = TRUE)` | Descending by the count that `bar * count` writes (largest first) |

## Duplicate categories {#duplicate-categories}

A table often holds several rows for one category, one per event or one per
year. The question is still how large each category is in total. Without a
transform, `bar` draws one bar per row, and rows that share a category share a
slot. This table has two rows each for USA and GBR:

```{r}
medals_dup <- data.frame(
  country = c("USA", "USA", "GBR", "GBR", "JPN"),
  gold    = c(10, 5, 8, 4, 6)
)
data(medals_dup) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  title("Duplicate rows: no transform")
```

*"Given the medals dup table: bars, x is country, y is gold."*

Every bar grows from zero, so the shorter ones are drawn inside the tallest. USA has
rows of 10 and 5, and its bar reads 10 rather than 15. Each bar is drawn
slightly translucent, so the color is darker where two bars overlap. For USA,
that darker band ends at 5, where the shorter bar stops. That band is the only
sign that a category has extra rows. When two rows hold the same value, the two
bars cover each other exactly. The whole bar is then darker than a bar of one
row, and no band shows, so the darker color is the only sign.

Use the `sum` transform to total the values per category first:

```{r}
data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) + title("Totals: bar * sum")
```

*"Given the medals dup table: bars derived by sum, x is country, y is gold,
ordered by gold, largest first."*

`sum` gives one number for each category. It reads every row that shares a
category and totals them. USA's 10 and 5 become 15, and GBR's 8 and 4 become
12. Five rows become three bars, one for each country, and the darker band is
gone.

`count`, from [Ordering bars](#ordering-bars), also draws one bar for each
category, but it measures something else. `sum` adds up the values in a column,
here `gold` on `y`. `count` counts the rows in each category and reads no
column. It writes its count on `y` itself, so `y(gold)` is refused ([What it
refuses](#what-it-refuses)). On this table it gives USA 2, GBR 2 and JPN 1, the
number of rows for each country:

```{r}
(data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold) +
   title("bar * sum + y(gold): gold added up")) |
  (data(medals_dup) + bar * count + x(country) +
     title("bar * count: rows counted"))
```

*"Given the medals dup table: bars derived by sum, x is country, y is gold,
beside bars derived by count, x is country."*

Use `sum` when you ask how much each category holds in total, such as gold
medals or sales. Use `count` when you ask how many rows each category has, such
as the countries of each continent.

## Negative values {#negative-values}

A bar can also point the other way, when a value is below zero, such as the
profit of a quarter that lost money. Every bar starts at zero. That rule made
the duplicate bars overlap, and it is also why a negative bar points down. So
you write nothing extra for a negative value:

```{r}
balance <- data.frame(quarter = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"),
                      profit  = c(12.0, -5.0, 8.0, -2.0))
data(balance) + bar + x(quarter) + y(profit) +
  title("Negative values grow downward from zero")
```

*"Given the balance table: bars, x is quarter, y is profit."*

To color the losses and the profits differently, you need a column that says
which is which, because gog does not decide which bars are losses. Map that
column with `color`, and let
[`palette()`](../style.qmd#palette-choosing-the-colors-a-mapping-uses) say
which colors the mapping uses. The table below sets the column's values by
hand. In practice you compute it from `profit` with one condition. Above zero
is a profit, and anything else is a loss.

```{r}
balance <- data.frame(
  quarter = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"),
  profit  = c(12.0, -5.0, 8.0, -2.0),
  result  = factor(c("profit", "loss", "profit", "loss"),
                   levels = c("loss", "profit"))
)
data(balance) + bar + x(quarter) + y(profit) + color(result) +
  palette(c("firebrick", "seagreen")) +
  title("Red below zero, green above")
```

*"Given the balance table: bars, x is quarter, y is profit, color by result,
with a palette of firebrick and seagreen."*

`palette()` assigns its colors in **category order**, and that is why `result`
carries a declared order here instead of being plain text. `palette()` does not
sort plain text, and `order()` does not move its colors: it assigns them in the
order the values first appear in the table. The first row here is a profit, so
the palette would give firebrick to the profits. Declaring the order as loss,
then profit, gives firebrick to the losses, and the legend lists them in that
order. The colors then stay with their results, even if next year's table
starts with a loss. R spells that with a factor's levels, Python with a pandas
`Categorical`, Julia with a `CategoricalArray`, and JavaScript with `ordered()`.
This is the same mechanism as [Declaring the order
of categories](../data.qmd#declaring-the-order-of-categories).

Red for loss and green for profit is one common convention. It is also the
hardest pair to separate for red-green color blindness, the most common kind.
Texture solves that and keeps the colors, by giving each result its own texture
as well as its own color. [Texture](#texture) below draws these bars that way,
and [Will it read in
gray?](../cookbook/three-or-more.qmd#will-it-read-in-gray) in the cookbook
applies the same idea to other plots.

## Horizontal bars {#horizontal-bars}

Sometimes the bars should be horizontal. The category names may be too long for
the bottom axis. Or there may be many categories, and a tall list of horizontal
bars reads more easily than a crowded row of vertical ones. Swap the bindings,
and put the categories on `y` and the measure on `x`:

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(gold) + y(country) +
  title("Categories on y: horizontal bars")
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is gold, y is country."*

If you know ggplot2's `coord_flip()` or matplotlib's `barh()`, gog has no such
word, because it would be a second way to say one thing. gog takes the
orientation from the bindings. The axis with the number is the one the bars
grow along, so their length is read on it. The axis with the
category is the one the bars are placed on, one slot each. Nothing else
changes: `order`, transforms such as `sum` and `bin`, `color` and `style()` all
behave as they do on vertical bars.

Horizontal bars help most when the category names are long. On a vertical axis
each label is written across the page, so it does not have to fit inside one
slot. The `departments` table holds the number of people (`headcount`) in each
of five departments of one company. The department names are long:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(departments)
```

```{r}
data(departments) + bar + x(headcount) + y(department) +
  order(headcount, desc = TRUE) +
  x_label("Headcount") +
  title("Long labels fit on a vertical axis")
```

*"Given the departments: bars, x is headcount, y is department, ordered by
headcount, largest first."*

`order` means the same thing in both orientations: the first category in sort
order takes the first slot. Descending puts the largest bar leftmost on a
vertical plot and topmost on a horizontal one.

Only one pair of columns says nothing about orientation: two columns of plain
numbers, such as `year` and `sales`. gog has one rule for that case: it measures
the column on `y` and draws vertical bars. So `x(year) + y(sales)` gives
vertical bars. Swapping the two bindings does not make the bars horizontal.
`x(sales) + y(year)` also gives vertical bars. The `quarterly` table, despite its
name, holds one sales figure for each year from 2005 to 2023. Both columns,
`year` and `sales`, hold numbers:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(quarterly)
```

```{r}
(data(quarterly) + bar + x(year) + y(sales) + title("x(year) + y(sales)")) |
  (data(quarterly) + bar + x(sales) + y(year) + title("x(sales) + y(year)"))
```

*"Given quarterly: bars, x is year, y is sales, beside bars, x is sales, y is
year."*

Both plots draw vertical bars. On the left, each bar's length is a year's sales.
On the right, each bar is drawn at its sales figure on `x`, and its length is
its year. Every year is about 2,000, which the axis writes as 2K, so all the
bars look the same height. A year is not an amount, so these lengths measure
nothing.

For horizontal bars, make the year categorical and put it on `y`. A column of
numbers becomes categorical when you
[declare the order](../data.qmd#declaring-the-order-of-categories) of its
values. Each year then gets a slot of its own, and the bars grow along `x`. The
`gm_eras` table holds 284 rows: one for each of 142 countries in 1957, and again
in 2007. It stores the year twice. `year` holds it as a number, and `era` holds
the same year as a category, made from `year` by declaring the order of its
values:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_eras)
```

Each year has 142 rows, one for each country, so `mean` averages their life
expectancies into one bar for each year:

```{r}
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(life) + y(era) +
  x_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("era on y: horizontal bars")
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean, x is life, y is era."*

The two bars grow along `x`: the mean life expectancy was about 52 years in 1957
and about 67 in 2007.

A column of dates needs no such step. A bar never measures a date, so dates on
`y` make the bars horizontal, as
[Bars on a date axis](../scales.qmd#bars-on-a-date-axis) shows.

A bar needs something to measure, so two categorical axes are refused.
[What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows that refusal.

## Texture {#texture}

The profit and loss bars in [Negative values](#negative-values) are red and
green, the pair hardest to distinguish for a reader with red-green color
blindness. Give each result its own texture as well, and that reader can
separate the bars without seeing color at all.

A bar's fill can carry a **texture**: lines or dots repeated across the bar, in
the bar's color. You set it with [`style(pattern = )`](../style.qmd). A texture does not
need color, so a hatched bar chart stays legible in grayscale or in a
black-and-white print:

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  style(pattern = "hatch") +
  title("A hatched bar reads without color")
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, with pattern hatch."*

`style(pattern = )` gives every bar in the layer the same texture. To give each
category its own texture, map a column with the [`pattern()`
channel](../channels.qmd#pattern), which does for texture what `shape()` does
for glyphs. The plot below maps the `texture` column with `pattern()`. Each bar
then shows one of the six fill textures, in this order: `"solid"` (the default,
a plain fill), `"hatch"`, `"crosshatch"`, `"stripes"`, `"grid"` and `"dots"`:

```{r}
textures <- data.frame(
  texture = c("solid", "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid", "dots"),
  height  = c(6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1)
)
data(textures) + bar + x(texture) + y(height) + pattern(texture) +
  x_label("") + y_label("") + title("The six fill textures")
```

*"Given the textures table: bars, x is texture, y is height, pattern by
texture."*

With more than six categories, the textures repeat: a seventh category gets
`"solid"` again. gog prints a message when that happens, and it suggests
`color()`, whose default palette has twenty colors, or `facet()`.

The [style chapter](../style.qmd) shows them beside the stroke patterns a line
takes, because `style(pattern = )` is one name whose values depend on the shape:
fill textures on a fill, stroke patterns on a stroke.

For the profit and loss bars, write `pattern(result)` beside `color(result)`.
The plot below uses the `balance` table from
[Negative values](#negative-values):

```{r}
data(balance) + bar + x(quarter) + y(profit) + color(result) +
  pattern(result) + palette(c("firebrick", "seagreen")) +
  title("A color and a texture for each result")
```

*"Given the balance table: bars, x is quarter, y is profit, color by result,
pattern by result, with a palette of firebrick and seagreen."*

The losses stay solid and the profits are hatched, so each result has its own
color and its own texture. Both channels read the same column, so one legend
shows both. A reader who cannot tell the red from the green can still tell the
solid bars from the hatched ones.

## Histogram {#histogram}

How are the world's life expectancies spread out, and where do most countries
fall? That is a question about one continuous column. To answer it, each bar
has to count the rows whose values fall in one range of that column. The `bin`
transform makes those ranges: it cuts the `x` axis into equal-width intervals,
called bins, and counts the rows in each. The `gapminder_2007` table, shown in
[Ordering bars](#ordering-bars), holds one life expectancy for each of 142
countries. Combine `bar` with `bin` to create a histogram:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) + y(count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life, y is count."*

`gapminder_2007` has no `count` column. `bin` writes the counts into a new
column named `count`, and `y(count)` refers to it. `count` is the only name
`y()` takes here. To label the axis in your own words, use `y_label()` ([The
name on a measure axis](../transforms.qmd#the-name-on-a-measure-axis)).

A bar's width is automatic, and it is the clearest way a histogram and a bar chart
differ on the page. A categorical bar fills 80% of its slot, which leaves a gap
between neighboring bars. That gap is what reads as separate categories. A
histogram cuts a continuous axis into adjacent intervals, so there is no
space between one bin and the next, and the bars *touch*. A thin line in the panel's
background color is drawn between neighboring bars, so each one can still be
seen. In both kinds of plot, the gold medal chart in [Basic usage](#basic-usage)
and this histogram, gog takes the bar's width from the axis, so you set nothing.

A bar can also be drawn on a continuous axis without `bin`. Its slot is then
the smallest distance between two neighboring values. Two countries here differ
in GDP by less than a dollar, so the slot is narrower than a pixel. gog then
draws every bar one pixel wide, at its own value:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  title("Bars on a continuous axis, without bin")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars, x is gdp, y is life."*

Each bar is one country. Where many countries have a similar GDP, the bars
touch and form one solid block. To see how the values spread, cut the axis into
bins with `bin`. To read each country's position, draw [`point`](point.qmd).

`bin` is not only for bars. Four other marks can draw the same bins,
and only the shape changes:

| Mark derived by `bin` | Shape |
|---|---|
| `point * bin` | one dot at the top of each bin |
| `line * bin` | the frequency polygon: straight lines through the bin centers |
| `area * bin` | the same polygon, filled to the baseline |
| `step * bin` | the staircase outline, drawn in [Step](step.qmd) |
| `bar * bin` | filled bars, the histogram above |

`zone * bin` and `surface * bin` cut two axes instead of one: the heatmap in
[Zone](zone.qmd) and the sheet in [Surface](surface.qmd).

The width of each bin decides what the histogram shows. With no argument, `bin`
picks the number of bins from the number of rows, by Sturges' rule
[@sturges1926]. The rule is simple: each time the number of rows doubles, the
histogram gets one more bin. So 100 rows get 8 bins, the 142 countries here get
9, and 1,000 rows get 11. Write a width with its name, `width =`, to cut the
axis in the column's own units. A number without a name always sets how many
bins there are, so `bin(5)` means five bins, not five years. Below,
`bin(width = 5)` cuts the axis into bins five years wide, and `bin(30)` into
thirty bins:

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(life) + y(count) +
   x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
   title("bin(width = 5): bins five years wide")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(life) + y(count) +
     x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
     title("bin(30): thirty bins"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin at width 5, x is life, y is count,
beside bars derived by bin into 30, x is life, y is count."*

Five-year bins give ten bars, and the shape is easy to read. Nearly half of the
countries, 70 of 142, fall between 70 and 80 years, and 39 of them between 70
and 75. Thirty bins are each about 1.4 years wide, so the counts are smaller and
change more from one bar to the next. One bin, from about 68.3 to 69.7 years,
holds no country, so 29 bars are drawn, with a gap the five-year bins hide.
Both plots write `y(count)`, so they share one count axis ([A column two plots
share](../composition.qmd#a-column-two-plots-share)), and the heights compare
directly: the tallest bar on the right holds 15 countries, and the tallest on
the left holds 39.

Use a width when each bin should cover a span that means something, such as
five years. Use a number of bins when you only want more detail or less.
[Choosing the bin count](../transforms.qmd#choosing-the-bin-count) explains why
a number without a name always means bins, and why gog refuses both at once.
[Choosing a width](../transforms.qmd#choosing-a-width) explains how to pick a
width for your own column.

A histogram can also be horizontal, by the rule in
[Horizontal bars](#horizontal-bars). Bind the column you are binning to `y`,
and the count is drawn along `x`. The sentence does not have to name the
count: `bin` computes it and draws it on the other axis, so `y(count)` in the
first histogram was optional:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same histogram, horizontal")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, y is life."*

### Where the bin edges fall {#where-the-bin-edges-fall}

This section reads the edges of the five-year histogram from
[Histogram](#histogram), so it is drawn again here:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(life) + y(count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("Bins five years wide")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin at width 5, x is life, y is count."*

Its first bin starts at 35, although the shortest life expectancy in the table
is 39.6. An edge is a value
where one bin ends and the next begins, and where the edges fall is a choice.
Each bar counts the rows between its two edges, such as the countries with a
life expectancy from 40 to 45. Suppose every edge were 2.5 years higher: the
bins would run from 37.5 to 42.5, from 42.5 to 47.5, and so on. A country at 41
years would then be counted in the bin from 37.5 to 42.5, not in the bin from
40 to 45. When countries change bins, the counts change, and the shape of the
histogram can change with them.

When you name a width, gog makes every edge a multiple of that width. The first
bin is the one that holds the smallest value. For these countries, the
five-year bins therefore run from 35 to 40, from 40 to 45, and so on up to 85.
In the plot above, every gridline from 40 to 80 is also a bin edge. A value exactly
on an edge is counted in the bin that starts there, so a life expectancy of 40
belongs to the bin from 40 to 45.

Edges on multiples of the width come from Leland Wilkinson's *The Grammar of
Graphics*, the book that gog is named after [@wilkinson2005]. He advises one
edge at zero. Every edge is then a multiple of the width, a round number that a
reader can find on the axis. He also says it should not be a strict rule,
because the edges change the shape of the histogram. Round edges are easy to
read, but other edges can give a smoother shape.

Wilkinson also treats one kind of column separately: a column that holds only
a few distinct values, such as the whole numbers from 0 to 10. With bins one
unit wide, every value of such a column falls exactly on an edge. The bar for 3
is then drawn from 3 to 4, not centered on 3. He gives each possible value a
bin of its own instead, centered on that value. In gog the nearest sentence
is `bar * count`, with one difference: it gives a slot to each value that
occurs, not to each possible value. Each bar is centered on its value. The width of each slot is the smallest distance between
two values that occur. A column that holds only 3 and 7 therefore gets two wide
bars side by side, with no empty slot between them. A column that holds 3, 4, 6
and 7 gets slots one unit wide, and the slot for 5, a value that never occurs,
is left empty. Below, `bar * bin(width = 1)` and `bar * count` draw the same
seven scores. The score 3 occurs once, 4 twice, 6 three times and 7 once:

```{r}
scores <- data.frame(score = c(3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7))
(data(scores) + bar * bin(width = 1) + x(score) + title("bar * bin(width = 1)")) |
  (data(scores) + bar * count + x(score) + title("bar * count"))
```

*"Given the scores table: bars derived by bin at width 1, x is score, beside bars
derived by count, x is score."*

On the left, each bar starts at its value. The bar for 3 runs from 3 to 4, so
the tick for 3 is at its left end, and a reader can take that bar for a score
of 3.5. On the right, each bar is centered on its value. No score is 5, so the
bin from 5 to 6 on the left is empty, and so is the slot for 5 on the right,
which has no tick. The left axis reaches 8 because the bin for 7 ends there.
For a column of a few whole numbers, use `bar * count`.

When you give the number of bins instead of a width, the edges are placed
differently. `bin(30)` divides the range from the smallest value to the largest
into thirty equal bins. For the 142 life expectancies, each bin is 1.43 years wide, as in
the `bin(30)` plot in [Histogram](#histogram), so the edges
are not round numbers. For round edges, name a width instead. With no argument,
`bin` chooses the number of bins itself, by Sturges' rule, so its edges also
run from the smallest value to the largest.

ggplot2 places its edges differently [@wickham2026ggplot2pkg]. Given a width,
ggplot2 puts the center of a bin at zero, where gog puts an edge. Its five-year
bins therefore run from 37.5 to 42.5, from 42.5 to 47.5, and so on. Given the
number of bins, ggplot2 makes each bin slightly wider than gog does. Its first
bin is then centered on the smallest value, and its last on the largest.
In ggplot2, a value exactly on an edge goes to the bin that ends there. Both packages count
every row once, but the bins cover different years, so the shapes differ. On
this table, gog's last five-year bin, 80 to 85, holds 13 countries, while
ggplot2's, 82.5 to 87.5, holds only Japan.

To put the edges anywhere else, state where the axis starts, and the first bin
starts there too. `x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5))` gives the five-year edges
that ggplot2 uses. [Scales](../scales.qmd#limits-stating-the-range-yourself)
explains `limits`.

### Overlaid histograms: one distribution per group {#overlaid-histograms}

The iris flowers table holds measurements of 150 flowers from three species. A
single histogram of all the flowers answers "how is petal length distributed?"
It cannot answer "how is it distributed *for each species*?" Add `color` and
the histogram *splits*: one histogram per category, cut on the same bins and
drawn in the same panel.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_flowers)
```

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Petal length by species")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, color by
species."*

The three histograms overlay. None of them is moved aside, and all three
measure from the same baseline. If the fills were opaque, the species drawn
last would hide the others wherever they overlap. So each bar is a translucent
fill under a solid outline in its own color. The outline is what keeps the
shape readable where the fills overlap. `setosa` is alone on the left and
reads clearly. `versicolor` and `virginica` overlap in the middle, and their
outlines still separate them. The groups share the same bins, so their bars
align, and an overlap in the plot is an overlap in the data.

`style(opacity = )` sets how faint the fill is; the outline stays solid whatever
you choose:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species) +
  style(opacity = 0.6) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A heavier fill: style(opacity = 0.6)")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, color by
species, with opacity 0.6."*

The outline is the group's color by default, but you can recolor it:
`style(border_color = )` sets the border, `style(border_size = )` its width. A
black border separates the overlapping fills, the way many overlaid histograms
are drawn. It also stays visible against the light panel, where a white one
disappears:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species) +
  style(border_color = "black", border_size = 1.5) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Black borders between the fills")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, color by
species, with border color black and border size 1.5."*

The fill and the outline are independent: a bar can be one color inside and
another at its edge, whether the fill was mapped (as here) or set. See
[Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd).

Or remove the outline entirely. `style(border_size = 0)` draws no border, so the
translucent fills overlap with nothing between them. This is the plainest
overlaid histogram:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species) +
  style(border_size = 0) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("No border: just the fills")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, color by
species, with border size 0."*

When the groups overlap so much that the outlines are hard to distinguish, give
each species its own panel instead. Adding
[`| facet(species)`](../faceting.qmd) to the sentence draws the same three
histograms side by side, on one shared scale. Or draw one smooth curve per
species, as in [Area](area.qmd#with-transforms). A curve has no bins, so two
species that overlap show as two lines that cross, not as two sets of bars
drawn over each other.

### The cumulative histogram {#the-cumulative-histogram}

A histogram's bar counts the rows in one bin. Add
[`cumulative`](../transforms.qmd#cumulative-the-running-total), and each bar
counts the rows in its bin and in every bin to its left. Each bar still grows
from zero, so its height is the total so far:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("bar * bin * cumulative: the cumulative histogram")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin and cumulative, x is life."*

The last bar is 142, every country in the table. Each bar is taller than the one
before it by the count of its own bin. The three largest rises, between about 68
and 83 years, come from the three bins that hold the most countries. The axis is
labeled "Cumulative", because each bar is a running total, not the count of one
bin.

## Grouped bars: side by side {#grouped-bars-side-by-side}

How did each continent's life expectancy change between 1957 and 2007? That is a
comparison inside each category, so each continent needs two bars, one per era.
A color split alone draws both bars in one slot, the shorter inside the taller.
To set them side by side as a **grouped bar chart**, add
[`dodge`](../transforms.qmd). Each group's bar narrows to share the slot, and
the split reads as a comparison within each category. The `gm_eras` table,
shown in [Horizontal bars](#horizontal-bars), holds the two years 1957 and 2007.
`mean` averages the countries into one value for each continent and era. `era`
is the column that splits each continent into two bars.

```{r}
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007")
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is
life, color by era."*

`dodge` is a collision modifier: it moves the bars rather than summarizing them,
so it composes with the statistic (`bar * mean * dodge` here, `bar * count *
dodge` for tallies). See [Transforms](../transforms.qmd) for all four collision
modifiers. A `text` layer over dodged bars takes the same `dodge` and a split of
its own, such as `group(era)`, so each number is printed on its own bar
([Labels on dodged bars](text.qmd#labels-on-dodged-bars)).

`mean` is the right statistic here, and gog will not choose it for you. Write
`sum` in its place and gog still draws it:

```{r}
data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  y_label("Sum of life expectancies") +
  title("Sum in place of mean: legal, and meaningless")
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by sum and dodge, x is continent, y is
life, color by era."*

Africa's fifty-two life expectancies for 2007 are added into one bar of 2,850
years. A sum of life expectancies has no meaning. You may write either
statistic. Which one is meaningful depends on what the column measures, and
[Law 8](../design-laws.qmd#law-8-pronounceable-usable) says why gog leaves
that choice to you.

### The gap beside each bar {#the-gap-beside-each-bar}

In a grouped bar chart, the two bars of each continent do not touch, as the
second plot below shows. The pair is given the width of one bar, and each bar an
equal part of it. Two bars that touch can read as one wide bar, so each bar
leaves a fifth of its part empty. `style(gap = )` sets that share, from 0, where
the bars touch, to just under 1, where almost nothing remains to draw. If you do
not set it, the gap is 0.2, a fifth. The four plots below set it to 0, leave it
unset, and set it to 0.5 and 0.9:

```{r}
((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
    style(gap = 0) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
    title("gap = 0: the two bars of a continent touch")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
      y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("gap unset: 0.2, the default")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
      style(gap = 0.5) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
      title("gap = 0.5: each bar half as wide as its part")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
      style(gap = 0.9) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
      title("gap = 0.9: each bar a tenth as wide as its part"))) +
  theme(height = 1150)
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is
life, color by era, with gap 0, above bars derived by mean and dodge, x is
continent, y is life, color by era, above the same with gap 0.5, above the
same with gap 0.9."*

With gap 0, the two bars of each continent touch. With 0.5, each bar is half as
wide as its part, and with 0.9, each bar is a tenth as wide as its part. On
dodged bars, `gap` acts only inside each bar's part, so in all four plots each
bar stays at the center of its part. A larger gap narrows each bar from both
sides, and the space between continents grows with it. The gap matters most
when the two bars share one color and differ only in their `pattern`.

The gap must be less than 1. At 1 nothing would be left to draw, so gog refuses
the sentence:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  style(gap = 1)
```

On a bar that is not dodged, `gap` is a share of the whole slot, and the default
is again a fifth. `style(gap = 0.5)` leaves half of each slot empty, so each bar
is half as wide as its slot. A histogram's bars leave no gap unless you set one,
because its bins are intervals that meet.

### Splitting without color {#splitting-without-color}

The plots below show each continent's mean life expectancy in 1957 and 2007 as
bars. An error bar on each bar shows the 95% confidence interval of its mean. A
second layer, `interval * confidence(0.95)`, draws the error bars
([Interval](interval.qmd#a-bar-with-its-error-bar)).

Bars with error bars are usually drawn in one of two ways. In the first, each
era's bars have their own color, and the error bars are black. In the second,
the bars are gray, and each era's error bars have their own color. The first is
more common, but neither is wrong. The choice is a matter of taste. Neither way
colors both layers by era. If it did, the part of each error bar below the mean
would be drawn on a bar of the same color and be hard to see.

In both ways, each era needs its own bar and its own error bar, so the layer in
one color still needs `group(era)`. `color(era)` does two things at once: it
splits each continent's rows by era, and it paints each era its own color.
[`group(era)`](../channels.qmd#group) does only the first. Without it, `dodge`
in that layer has no groups to set side by side, and gog refuses the sentence.
So the layer with the colors takes `color(era)`, and the layer in one color
takes `group(era)` and `style(color = )`. A channel such as `color` or `group`,
written after a mark, reaches only the nearest mark before it, so each layer has
its own. `x` and `y` are positions, which every layer shares, so writing them
last changes nothing
([Which marks a channel reaches](../grammar.qmd#which-marks-a-channel-reaches)):

```{r}
(data(gm_eras) +
   bar * mean * dodge + color(era) +
   interval * confidence(0.95) * dodge + group(era) +
   style(center = FALSE, color = "black") +
   x(continent) + y(life) + y_label("Mean life expectancy (years)") +
   title("Colored bars, black error bars")) /
  (data(gm_eras) +
     bar * mean * dodge + group(era) + style(color = "lightgray") +
     interval * confidence(0.95) * dodge + color(era) + style(center = FALSE) +
     x(continent) + y(life) + y_label("Mean life expectancy (years)") +
     title("Gray bars, colored error bars")) +
  theme(height = 900)
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, colored by era, and
also intervals derived by confidence at 95% and dodge, grouped by era, with
center off, colored black, x is continent, y is life, above bars derived by mean
and dodge, grouped by era, colored lightgray, and also intervals derived by
confidence at 95% and dodge, colored by era, with center off, x is continent, y
is life."*

`style(center = FALSE)` leaves out each error bar's center dot, because the bar
already marks the mean. In the upper plot, the black error bars are clear on
both colors, below the mean as well as above it.

A bar takes `group` only when a statistic, `dodge` or `stack` acts on its rows.
With `group(era)`, a statistic such as `mean` computes one value for each era in
a slot, not one for the whole slot. `dodge` sets each era's bar beside the
others, and
[`stack`](../transforms.qmd#stack-piled-up-not-side-by-side) sets it on top of
them ([Stacked bars](#stacked-bars-piled-up), below). With none of these, gog
refuses `group` ([What it refuses](#what-it-refuses)). The four plots below show
why. They draw the same table on the same axes and differ in their transform.
The top-left plot, with no transform, also has no `group(era)`, because gog
refuses it there:

```{r}
((data(gm_eras) + bar + x(continent) + y(life) + title("bar: one bar per row")) |
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + group(era) +
      title("bar * dodge: eras apart, countries overlap"))) /
  ((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) + group(era) +
      title("bar * mean: two means, one slot")) |
     (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + group(era) +
        title("bar * mean * dodge: two means, side by side"))) +
  theme(height = 750)
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars, x is continent, y is life, beside bars derived
by dodge, x is continent, y is life, grouped by era; above bars derived by mean,
x is continent, y is life, grouped by era, beside bars derived by mean and
dodge, x is continent, y is life, grouped by era."*

With no transform, gog draws one bar for each row. The 284 rows of `gm_eras`
become 284 bars, and the bars of one continent overlap in one slot, the shorter
ones inside the tallest. Only the tallest bar in each slot can be seen, so the
plot shows each continent's longest life expectancy, as in
[Duplicate categories](#duplicate-categories). Where a bar goes depends only on
its continent, not on its era, so `group(era)` would leave this plot exactly as
it is. With `dodge` and no statistic, the two eras' bars are set side by side,
but each side still holds one bar per country, the shorter ones inside the
tallest. With `mean` and no `dodge`, each era gets one bar, but the two share one
slot. Each bar is slightly translucent, so in each slot the color is darker where
the 1957 bar and the taller 2007 bar overlap. With `mean * dodge`, each era gets
one bar, and the two are drawn side by side. In both dodged plots, the left bar
of each slot is 1957 and the right bar is 2007.

A stack can be split by `group` too, when each bar's total matters more than its
segments. Every segment then has the same color, so gog separates them with a
thin line in the panel's background color. It is the line that separates the
bars of a [histogram](#histogram). The `channel_sales` table holds each
quarter's `revenue` from two ways of selling. Its `channel` column names them,
Retail and Online. The table has one row for each quarter and way of selling, so
`stack` needs no statistic:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(channel_sales)
```

```{r}
data(channel_sales) + bar * stack + x(quarter) + y(revenue) + group(channel)
```

*"Given the channel sales table: bars derived by stack, x is quarter, y is
revenue, grouped by channel."*

Each bar's height is the quarter's total. Retail comes first in the table, so it
is the lower segment of each bar. The thin line marks where the retail revenue
ends and the online revenue begins. No color or legend tells the two segments
apart. When the reader needs to know which is which, another layer has to label
them.

## Stacked bars: piled up {#stacked-bars-piled-up}

Sometimes the question is the total as well as the parts: how much is there
altogether, and how much of it does each group hold? A color split can be
placed a second way. Instead of side by side, [`stack`](../transforms.qmd) piles
the groups on top of each other. Each bar's height becomes the category's total
across the groups, and the segments read as parts of a whole:

```{r}
data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(continent) + y(population) + color(era) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked")
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by sum and stack, x is continent, y is
population, color by era."*

`dodge` sets the groups side by side, all on one baseline; `stack` piles them
into one bar, whose height is their total. Use `stack` when the parts add to a
meaningful total (populations, counts, revenue), and `dodge` when you are
comparing the groups. The two examples also use different statistics. You stack
the `sum` of population, because quantities add, and you dodge the `mean` of
life, because averages do not.

[Grouped bars](#grouped-bars-side-by-side) drew `sum` where `mean` was the
right statistic, and the opposite works the same way. gog checks that a sentence
is well-formed, not that its plot makes sense, and choosing the statistic is
your decision ([Law 8](../design-laws.qmd#law-8-pronounceable-usable)). Write
`mean` in place of `sum`, and gog draws it, piling two averages into a bar that
reads as their total:

```{r}
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * stack + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy, stacked") +
  title("Mean in place of sum: legal, and meaningless")
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and stack, x is continent, y is
life, color by era."*

Oceania's pile reaches about 151 years. A stack reads as parts of a total, so it
makes sense only when its values add up, as populations do.

### The 100% stacked bar {#the-100-stacked-bar}

The population stack answers two questions at once: how large each total is,
and how it splits. The totals differ so much that the small continents' splits
are hard to read. Asia's 1957 and 2007 populations add up to 5.4 billion, and
Oceania's add up to 0.04 billion. The axis is scaled for Asia, so Oceania's bar is
too short to show its split at all. When the split is the question and the
total is not, ask for shares. `stack(share = TRUE)` divides each segment by its
own bar's total. Each segment then shows its group's share of the bar, a number
from 0 to 1. Every bar reaches 1, so all the splits are on one scale and can be
compared across continents:

```{r}
data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE) + x(continent) + y(population) +
  color(era) + title("Each continent's 1957/2007 split, filled to one")
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by sum and stack as shares, x is
continent, y is population, color by era."*

With every bar at 1, the question changes. The population stack compared the
two eras inside one continent, and only for the large ones. This plot compares
the splits across continents: which population grew the most between the two
eras. Africa's population grew the most. Of its two-era total, 78% falls in
2007 and 22% in 1957, so it more than tripled. Europe's grew the least: 57% of
its total falls in 2007, the closest any continent comes to an even split.
Neither number can be read from the population stack above. This plot does not
show the totals at all, which is why Oceania's bar is now as tall as Asia's.
Each plot answers one of the two questions. `stack`
says how much each continent has, and `stack(share = TRUE)` says how it splits.
When you need both answers, draw both plots.

The axis is labeled `Share` rather than `Population`, because every value is
now a fraction of its bar's total. `Share` alone does not say a share of what,
so name it yourself with `y_label("Share of two-era population")`.
`stack(share = TRUE)` is not
[`proportion`](../transforms.qmd#proportion-relative-frequency) under another
name. The two divide by different totals. `proportion` divides by the whole
plot's total, so its bars still show how large each category is. This one
divides by the bar's own total.

`stack(share = TRUE)` works the same way on a histogram of `gapminder_2007`,
the table shown in [Ordering bars](#ordering-bars). `bin` cuts the axis into
bins, and each segment is then divided by its own bin's total. The question
changes from how many countries fall in each bin to which continents those
countries are in:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) * stack(share = TRUE) + x(life) +
  color(continent) + x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  y_label("Share of the countries in the bin") +
  title("Each continent's share of each five-year bin, 2007")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin at width 5 and stack as shares, x is
life, color by continent."*

Below 60 years, more than 80% of the countries in each bin are in Africa. From
60 to 70, Asia has the largest share, and Africa and the Americas hold the rest.
Europe first appears in the bin from 70 to 75. From 75 to 85, about half of the
countries in each bin are European. Oceania's two countries both fall in the
last bin.

This plot hides what the five-year histogram in [Histogram](#histogram) shows: how many
countries each bin holds. The bin from 35 to 40 holds one country and the bin
from 70 to 75 holds 39, but both bars reach 1. When the counts matter, draw that
histogram beside this one. In ggplot2, `stack(share = TRUE)` is written
`position = "fill"`. Its five-year bins have other edges, so its bars differ
([Where the bin edges fall](#where-the-bin-edges-fall)).

## Grouped, stacked or 100% stacked? {#grouped-stacked-or-100-stacked}

You have now seen three ways to place a color split. `dodge` sets the groups
side by side, `stack` piles them up, and `stack(share = TRUE)` piles them up as
shares. Each way makes one question easy to answer and another question hard,
so the choice depends on the question your reader must answer. To see the
difference, draw one table all three ways.

The `titanic` table counts the people aboard the Titanic, the ship that sank in
1912. Each row is one combination of `class`, `sex`, `age` and `survived`, and
`n` says how many people match it, sometimes none. Each row already holds a
count, so the plots add up `n` with `sum` rather than counting rows with
`count`. `color(survived)` then splits each class into the people who survived
and the people who died.

One legend explains all three plots below, so `legend = FALSE` leaves it out of
the first two. The third plot asks for 330 pixels of the arrangement's width
with `theme(width = 330)`, so its legend has room.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(titanic)
```

```{r}
((data(titanic) + bar * sum * dodge + x(class) + y(n) +
    color(survived, legend = FALSE) + y_label("People") + title("dodge")) |
  (data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack + x(class) + y(n) +
    color(survived, legend = FALSE) + title("stack")) |
  (data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE) + x(class) + y(n) +
    color(survived) + y_label("Share of the class") +
    title("stack(share = TRUE)") + theme(width = 330))) +
  theme(height = 360)
```

*"Given titanic: bars derived by sum and dodge, x is class, y is n, color by
survived, without a legend, beside bars derived by sum and stack, x is class, y
is n, color by survived, without a legend, beside bars derived by sum and stack
as shares, x is class, y is n, color by survived."*

All three plots start from the same eight sums: the survivors and the dead in each class. The first
two read `n` on the y axis, so they share one axis, drawn once at the left. That
axis is sized for the crew's total, 885, which is why the dodge plot leaves room
above its tallest bar, 673. The third plot divides each segment by its class's
total, so it draws a separate axis, from 0 to 1. `y_label()` names that axis, as
in [The 100% stacked bar](#the-100-stacked-bar).

Each plot answers one kind of question best, and each one hides something. For
each plot, the table gives both:

| Plot | Answers best | Hides |
|---|---|---|
| `dodge` | Did more people survive or die in each class? Did more people die in third class or in the crew? | Each class's total. To see it, you must add two bar heights yourself. |
| `stack` | How many people were in each class, and how many of them survived? | How the deaths compare across classes. The segments of the dead start at different heights. |
| `stack(share = TRUE)` | In which class was a person most likely to survive? | How many people each class held. Second class held 285 people and the crew 885, but both bars reach 1. |

`dodge` answers its questions because every bar starts at zero, so any two
bars can be compared by height. In the first plot, for example, first class is
the only class with more survivors than dead. In `stack`, only the bottom
group, the survivors, starts at zero. `stack(share = TRUE)` makes every bar
reach 1, so each segment's height is its share of the class.

The crew and first class show why the choice depends on the question. If you
count the survivors, as the first two plots do, the two have nearly the same
number: 212 against 203. If you divide by each class's total, as the third plot
does, they are far apart: 24% of the crew survived, against 62% of first class.
Both facts are true, and each plot shows only one of them. When the reader needs
more than one answer, draw more than one plot, as this section does.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a bar takes and
the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("bar")
```

The plots below show every transform a bar takes. Within a figure the plots
differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any
other change.

**Counting.** `count` and `proportion` tally the rows at each value of `x`, on a
category or a number. `bin` and `density` work on a number. `bin` counts the
rows in each interval, and `density` estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely
the rows lie along the axis. Each puts its result on the axis you leave empty.
The top two plots put `continent` on `x`, and the plot below them puts `life`.
On a bar, `bin` gives the [histogram](#histogram):

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + title("bar * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent) +
     title("bar * proportion"))) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) + title("bar * bin"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, beside bars
derived by proportion, x is continent; above bars derived by bin, x is life."*

The density is drawn in a figure of its own. In one figure with the `bin` plot,
the two would share one `life` axis that covers only the range of the rows, and
the density's tails would be cut off ([A plot cut by a shared
axis](../composition.qmd#a-plot-cut-by-a-shared-axis)). `density` gives one bar at each
place where the curve was computed, with a gap between neighboring bars, as bars
beside a category have. The places run a little past the data on both sides,
where the curve is close to zero, so the outermost bars are too short to see.
The plots below leave `places` at its default, 256, and set it to 32:

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density + x(life) +
   title("bar * density: 256 places, the default")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density(places = 32) + x(life) +
     title("bar * density(places = 32)"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by density, x is life, beside bars derived
by density at 32 places, x is life."*

At 256 places the bars touch and form one shape. At 32, the gaps between them
can be seen.

Look at the `y` axis of the five plots above, from `bar * count` to
`bar * density(places = 32)`. None of the five sentences writes `y()`, yet each
`y` axis has a name: Count, Proportion, Count, Density and Density. The table
has no column by those names. Each transform writes one, and `y` draws it.
`count` and `bin` write `count`, the number of rows at each value or in each
interval. `proportion` writes `proportion`, each count's share of all the rows.
`density` writes `density`, the height of the estimated curve. The axis is
labeled with the column's name, capitalized, as [The name on a measure
axis](../transforms.qmd#the-name-on-a-measure-axis) explains.

**Summaries.** The six summaries reduce the rows at each value of `x` to one
value, so they need a number on `y`. Each bar then reaches that value. `sum`
reads `population`, because only an amount has a total that means something.
The other five read `life`. They give the mean, the median, the largest and the
smallest value, and `quantile(0.9)` gives the value that nine tenths of the rows
fall below:

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(continent) + y(population) +
    title("bar * sum")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
     title("bar * mean")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * median + x(continent) + y(life) +
     title("bar * median"))) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * max + x(continent) + y(life) +
      title("bar * max")) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * min + x(continent) + y(life) +
        title("bar * min")) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * quantile(0.9) + x(continent) + y(life) +
        title("bar * quantile(0.9)")))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum, x is continent, y is population,
beside bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, beside bars derived by
median, x is continent, y is life; above bars derived by max, x is continent, y
is life, beside bars derived by min, x is continent, y is life, beside bars
derived by quantile at 0.9, x is continent, y is life."*

The five plots that read `life` share one scale, so their heights can be
compared from plot to plot. [Duplicate categories](#duplicate-categories) shows
why a bar needs a summary when a table holds several rows for one category.

**Fitted lines.** `smooth` and `straight` need a number on each axis. They fit a
line to the rows, each placed at its `x` and its `y`. `smooth` follows the
shape of the data, and `straight` is the least-squares line. A fitted line is
usually drawn with `line`, as a curve or a straight line over the points
([Smoothed trend line](line.qmd#smoothed-trend-line)). gog draws it on a bar as
well, which is legal but unusual, as bars at evenly spaced places along `x`, and
their tops trace the line.
There are 100 places unless you set `places`, and the first two plots ask
for 24, so that each bar can be seen.

**Running total.** `cumulative` adds each value to the ones before it along the
axis. After `bin`, it gives the [cumulative
histogram](#the-cumulative-histogram). The third plot reads the `actuals` table,
with `year` on `x` and `sales` on `y`. The table holds one year of sales in each
row:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(actuals)
```

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * smooth(places = 24) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   title("bar * smooth(places = 24)")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * straight(places = 24) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
     title("bar * straight(places = 24)")) |
  (data(actuals) + bar * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) +
     title("bar * cumulative"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by smooth at 24 places, x is gdp, y is
life, beside bars derived by straight at 24 places, x is gdp, y is life; beside
bars from the actuals,
derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales."*

**Collision modifiers.** Collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on
top of one another. On a bar they place the
bars that would share one slot. `dodge` sets them side by side, and `stack`
piles them up. `stack(share = TRUE)` also piles them up, and divides each piece
by its bar's total. All three need the rows split by `color`, `pattern` or
`group`, so that each slot holds more than one bar. The `gm_eras` table holds one row for each country
in each era, so each plot also needs a summary before the modifier. The `dodge`
plot averages `life`. The two stacks add up `population`, because only an amount
has a total that means something:

```{r}
(((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
     title("bar * mean * dodge")) |
    (data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(continent) + y(population) +
       color(era) + title("bar * sum * stack"))) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE) + x(continent) +
      y(population) + color(era) + title("bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE)"))) +
  theme(height = 800)
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is
life, color by era, beside bars derived by sum and stack, x is continent, y is
population, color by era; above bars derived by sum and stack as shares, x is
continent, y is population, color by era."*

[Grouped bars](#grouped-bars-side-by-side) and [Stacked
bars](#stacked-bars-piled-up) explain each one in full.

A bar refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. The pair transforms
give `y` a low and a high at each value of `x`, which [`interval`](interval.qmd),
[`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd), [`line`](line.qmd) and [`step`](step.qmd) take. `jitter` moves each point a short way along the
categorical axis, and only [`point`](point.qmd) takes it. `repel` moves
[`text`](text.qmd) labels off each other. `partition`, `flow` and `cluster` lay
out rectangles, bands and branches, which [`zone`](zone.qmd), [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd) and
[`path`](path.qmd) draw. `layout` places a network, which [`point`](point.qmd), [`text`](text.qmd) and
[`edge`](edge.qmd) draw.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

A setting changes how every bar looks without reading a column, and each mark
takes its own. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are a bar's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("bar")
```

A bar has no `size`, and that is deliberate. Its value sets its length, and its
slot sets its width, so a `size` in pixels would be a second, conflicting width.
`gap` does not conflict, because it is a share of the slot: it sets how much of
the slot the bar leaves empty ([The gap beside each bar](#the-gap-beside-each-bar)).
A bar is a shape with an inside and an outline, so it does have a border.

A fill, a texture and a border compose, so one layer can carry all three. The
plot uses the `medals` table, shown in [Basic usage](#basic-usage):

```{r}
data(medals) + bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold) +
  style(color = "goldenrod", pattern = "crosshatch",
        border_color = "black", border_size = 1) +
  y_label("Gold medals") + title("A fill, a texture, and a border")
```

*"Given the medals: bars derived by sum, x is country, y is gold, colored
goldenrod, with pattern crosshatch, border color black and border size 1."*

The settings table above lists the six fill textures a bar takes. A `line` takes
five stroke patterns instead, and only `"solid"` is in both lists.

The histogram's bins are not a setting. `bin(30)` and `bin(width = 5)` belong
to the transform, because they change what is counted, not how a bar is drawn.
[Histogram](#histogram) shows `bin(width = 5)`, and [Choosing the bin
count](../transforms.qmd#choosing-the-bin-count) shows both.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

The five refusals below have different causes. The first two belong to the
transform rather than the mark: `bin` needs a continuous axis to cut, and `count`
computes the number it draws. The other three belong to the mark: a bar is a
fill rather than a stroke, a bar needs a number to measure, and on a bar with no
transform, splitting by `group` would change nothing.

Binning cuts a continuous axis into intervals, so there is nothing for it to cut
on a categorical one:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(continent)
```

To count the rows in each category's slot, use `count`. The refusal names
`bar * count` rather than drawing empty bins.

The second refusal comes from `count` itself. On `y`, `count` draws the number
of rows in each slot, so a column named on `y` would never be read. gog refuses
it, because the axis would be titled `life` while its numbers are counts:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + y(life)
```

To summarize `life` in each slot, use a statistic that reads it, such as
`bar * mean`. `y(count)` in the [first histogram](#histogram) is accepted, because it names
the column that `bin` writes.

The third refusal is about texture. A bar is a filled shape, so it takes the fill
textures, such as `"hatch"`. `"dashed"` is a stroke pattern:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) + style(pattern = "dashed")
```

A bar's outline takes a color and a width, never a stroke pattern. `border_color` and
`border_size` are the only two settings the outline has.

Two categorical positions are the fourth refusal. The axis with the category
places the bars, one slot each, and the axis with the number measures how far
they reach, as [Horizontal bars](#horizontal-bars) explained. With a category
on both, there is no length left to draw:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(country)
```

The message names two fixes: put a number on one axis, or count the rows per
category with `bar * count`.

The fifth refusal is `group` on a bar with no transform. Each row of the table
is already its own bar, so splitting the rows by era would change nothing in
the picture. The plot titled *bar: one bar per row*, in
[Splitting without color](#splitting-without-color), shows that picture. With
`group(era)` added, gog refuses the sentence:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_eras) + bar + x(continent) + y(life) + group(era)
```

The message names three fixes. The first, `dodge`, sets the two eras' bars side
by side in each slot. It is enough when the table holds one row for each bar,
as `channel_sales` does. `gm_eras` holds one row for each country, so it needs
the second fix as well: a statistic such as `mean`, as in
[Splitting without color](#splitting-without-color). The third fix writes
`color(era)` in place of `group(era)`, which gives each era its own color and a
legend. On this table it still needs `mean * dodge` to draw one bar for each era.

## In short {#in-short}

The axis with the category places the bars, and the axis with the number
measures them. A bar's length is its value, and that axis reaches
zero unless you state your own `limits`. Without a transform one bar is drawn
per row, and rows sharing a category overlap in one slot. A categorical bar
fills 80% of its slot unless you set `gap`. A histogram bar fills its whole bin,
and `bin()` decides how wide a bin is.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

The gap on each side of a bar says that the categories are separate. When the
positions are continuous, such as the years of a sales series, the `area` mark ([Area](area.qmd))
joins each value to the next and fills the region below them, with no gaps.
